items.title: A perfume molecule takes a very long time to reach the door
items.claim: Spritz perfume at one end of a still room. The molecules diffuse through the air. The mean speed of an air molecule is about 500 m/s. The perfume should cross a 5 m room in 10 milliseconds. It actually takes minutes to hours.
items.prompt: Why is diffusion so slow if individual molecules are so fast?

options.text: Diffusion has nothing to do with molecular motion
Each molecule collides with others about 10 to the 10 times per second, so it executes a random walk; mean displacement scales as the square root of time, not linearly
The perfume is heavier than air

items.reveal_title: Random walk — square-root scaling instead of linear
items.reveal:
Mean free path in air is about 70 nanometres. A perfume molecule's velocity changes direction roughly every 10 to the minus 10 seconds. Its position evolves as a random walk: net displacement after time t scales as the square root of (D times t), where D is the diffusion coefficient.

For air at room temperature D is about 10 to the minus 5 m squared per second. To cross 5 metres by diffusion: t equals 5 squared over D, which is roughly 2.5 million seconds — about a month.

In practice convection moves perfume around your room in seconds. Diffusion is far too slow for everyday scales. But it dominates inside cells (microns) — and over micron scales it takes only milliseconds.
items.why: Linear-time intuition for travel is wrong for random walks. Diffusion gets dramatically slower as scales increase, because of the square-root law.

items.title: Water has the highest specific heat of any common liquid
items.claim: Raising the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1°C requires 4180 J. The same energy raises 1 kg of iron by 9.3°C, 1 kg of mercury by 30°C. Water is exceptionally hard to warm — and to cool.
items.prompt: What makes water's heat capacity so high?

options.text: Heat in water is shared between molecular vibrations, rotations, and the breaking and re-forming of hydrogen bonds; the hydrogen-bond network absorbs huge amounts of energy with only modest temperature rise
Water is denser than most liquids

items.reveal:
When you heat water, energy doesn't just speed molecules up. A significant fraction goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds — about 23 kJ/mol per bond, with each molecule forming up to four.

This is why coastal climates are mild: oceans absorb and release heat slowly. The Gulf Stream warms northwest Europe by carrying tropical heat north. Water's heat capacity buffers the climate.

It's also why sweating cools so effectively: evaporating 1 g of water absorbs 2260 J (latent heat of vaporisation) — far more than the same mass of any common solvent. And why ice cubes drop drinks' temperatures so quickly: melting 1 g of ice absorbs 334 J (latent heat of fusion).
items.why: Specific heat is taught as a number to look up. It is a measure of how many ways a substance can absorb energy at the molecular level.

items.title: The laws of physics don't tell time which way to run
items.claim: Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations and the Schrödinger equation all look the same if you reverse time. So why do we remember the past but not the future, and why does milk mix into coffee but never unmix?
items.prompt: Where does the arrow of time come from?

options.text: Gravity defines a preferred time direction
The second law of thermodynamics — entropy increases with time, statistically — but only because the universe started in an extremely low-entropy state and is far from equilibrium
Time has a built-in direction physicists haven't found yet
We perceive time directionally; physics doesn't have a preferred direction

items.reveal_title: Boltzmann's H-theorem and the low-entropy past
items.reveal:
Microscopic laws are time-reversible. But there are vastly more disordered configurations than ordered ones. Starting from any low-entropy state, the overwhelmingly likely evolution is toward higher entropy.

The question becomes: why did the universe start in such a low-entropy state? The Big Bang and the smoothness of the early universe set up an enormous entropy 'budget' that has been depleting ever since.

We remember the past because forming a memory increases entropy. We can't 'remember' the future because that would correspond to entropy decreasing in the brain.

The 'arrow of time' is an emergent statistical property of an initial condition — not a fundamental law.
items.why: Time feels like it has an obvious direction. Physically, that direction is a cosmological accident, not a fundamental property of time itself.
